name: Lunar Orbiter Program
short_status: Five orbiters flown 1966 to 1967, all five successful; each was deliberately crashed into the Moon at the end of its mission, the last on January 31, 1968.
tagline: NASA · United States · Orbiter · 1966 · The space race Success

facts.label: Program approval
facts.value: Approved by NASA Associate Administrator Robert C. Seamans on 30 August 1963; managed by NASA's Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia

facts.label: Builder
facts.value: The Boeing Company of Seattle won the contract on 7 May 1964 to build five spacecraft, each about 850 pounds (386 kg) with a 145-pound imaging system, four solar panels and a 36-inch dish antenna

facts.label: Camera system
facts.value: Eastman Kodak built the dual-lens imaging system (610mm narrow-angle plus 80mm wide-angle) based on classified military reconnaissance-satellite technology; it exposed 70mm film, developed it onboard with a Kodak Bimat semidry process, scanned it, and radioed the images to Earth

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: The five orbiters photographed 99% of the Moon at a resolution of 60 meters or better, including the far side, with high-resolution detail down to about 1 meter at the lowest passes

facts.label: Outcome
facts.value: All five missions succeeded and met their objectives, an unusual clean sweep for a 1960s US lunar program (Ranger and Surveyor both lost spacecraft)

facts.label: Two-phase plan
facts.value: The first three orbiters surveyed 20 candidate Apollo landing sites from low-inclination orbits; the last two switched to broad scientific mapping from high near-polar orbits, with Lunar Orbiter 4 imaging the entire near side and Lunar Orbiter 5 completing far-side coverage

facts.label: Lunar Orbiter 1 firsts
facts.value: Launched 10 August 1966; became the first US spacecraft to orbit the Moon on 14 August 1966, and on 23 August 1966 took the first photograph of Earth from the vicinity of the Moon, an unplanned shot on its 16th orbit

facts.label: Copernicus image
facts.value: Lunar Orbiter 2's oblique view of the crater Copernicus, taken in November 1966 from about 28 miles up, was dubbed by the news media "one of the great pictures of the century" for revealing the Moon as a world of dramatic topography rather than a flat map

facts.label: First full Earth
facts.value: Lunar Orbiter 5 captured the first photograph of the whole Earth from space on 8 August 1967, from lunar orbit

facts.label: Why they were crashed
facts.value: Each orbiter was deliberately commanded to impact the Moon at end of mission so its transmitter could not interfere with tracking and communications for the next Lunar Orbiter and to clear the orbital environment

facts.label: Lunar Orbiter 1 impact
facts.value: Impacted the far side on 29 October 1966 during its 577th orbit; NSSDCA lists the site as about 6.35 degrees N, 160.71 degrees E (NASA's mission page gives another published figure, 6 degrees 42 minutes N, 162 degrees E)

facts.label: Site selection payoff
facts.value: By April 1967 planners had narrowed the Moon to eight preliminary Apollo landing sites from Lunar Orbiter imagery, including the site that became Apollo 11's Tranquility Base

timeline: NASA approves the Lunar Orbiter program to scout Apollo landing sites; Langley Research Center will manage it
Lunar Orbiter 1 launches on an Atlas-Agena D from Cape Canaveral
Lunar Orbiter 1 enters lunar orbit, the first US spacecraft to circle the Moon
Lunar Orbiter 1 takes the first photograph of Earth from the vicinity of the Moon, more than two years before Apollo 8's color Earthrise
Lunar Orbiter 1 is deliberately crashed into the far side on its 577th orbit, near 6.35 N, 160.71 E, so its radio cannot interfere with Lunar Orbiter 2
Lunar Orbiter 2's oblique view of Copernicus, later called "one of the great pictures of the century," is taken from about 28 miles up
Lunar Orbiter 3 launches; it later photographs the Surveyor 1 lander sitting on the surface
Lunar Orbiter 4 launches into a high near-polar orbit and maps essentially the entire lunar near side
Lunar Orbiter 5, the last of the series, launches to finish far-side mapping and survey later Apollo sites
Lunar Orbiter 5 photographs the whole Earth from lunar orbit, the first full-Earth image from space
Lunar Orbiter 5 is deliberately crashed into the Moon, the last of the five commanded impacts, near 2.79 S, 83.01 W
The Lunar Orbiter Image Recovery Project at NASA Ames restores the original data tapes and re-releases the Earthrise and other frames at modern quality
